strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated, underexplored problem: instance-level (personal-object) manipulation for frozen VLAs, which existing benchmarks and baselines do not cover. The formulation (grounding + visual prompting as an input-side adapter) is clear and sensible.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this type of work: two newly constructed simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench) plus a real-world tabletop benchmark on a SO-101 arm with 8 object categories, multiple tasks, and both selection and pick-and-place settings.

Baselines are thoughtfully designed and strengthened: the token-learning (Soft Prompt) baseline is adapted from Yo'LLaVA with oracle hard negatives drawn from the deployment distribution, achieving >95% recognition accuracy, so the comparison against VAP is credible rather than a strawman. The appendix analysis of token embedding transfer (cosine/CKA/kNN metrics) and attention heatmaps is a valuable contribution in itself.

The error-case taxonomy (wrong single-view grounding, cross-view inconsistency, correct prompt but failed manipulation) is honest and informative, with quantitative breakdowns (Table 6/9), and the limitations (segmentation quality, cross-view consistency, single-object short-horizon scope) are candidly discussed in the conclusion and Appendix E.
Runtime analysis (Table 5) shows the perception overhead is modest (~10% per-step), addressing a practical deployment concern for a training-free adapter.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: VAP is essentially a pipeline of off-the-shelf components (Grounding DINO for detection, DINOv2 embedding matching, SAM2 segmentation/tracking, a semi-transparent tint overlay, and a template-based instruction rewrite). The core idea—highlight the target and rewrite 'my X' to 'the red X'—is an intuitive composition of prior visual-prompting and personalization work rather than a new technique.

There is no component ablation isolating the contributions of (a) the pixel-space highlight, (b) the instruction rewrite, and (c) the tracking, e.g., comparing highlight-only vs. rewrite-only vs. both. Since the rewrite alone effectively reduces the task to a color/attribute disambiguation problem that hard prompts partly solve (see the bottle task, where Hard Prompt (Long) is competitive), it is unclear how much of the gain comes from the visual highlight specifically. A tint-color ablation (robustness to choosing a tint matching a distractor's color) is also missing.

Statistical reporting is thin: no confidence intervals or variance across the 10 evaluation runs is reported in Tables 2–4, and real-world results average only 20 trials per task. Given the differences between baselines are sometimes modest (e.g., Table 4, cat figurine: 44.4 vs 51.6), significance is hard to assess.

The evaluation scope is narrow relative to the framing: scenes contain one personal object and at most two same-category distractors, tasks are short-horizon tabletop selections/placements, and CMR can inflate from incidental object motion (as the authors themselves note for Task 6). The paper's real-world motivation (cluttered homes) is not matched by the evaluation conditions.

Some benchmark details raise questions: Personalized-VLABench episodes (125 x 10) differ from the stated 250 episodes in Table 1, and the inconsistency between Table 1 (#Episodes) and Table 9 episode counts is unexplained; reference images are captured from the same real cameras used at test time, which may overstate robustness compared to user-supplied photos taken in arbitrary conditions.

Reproducibility is not clearly committed: no statement about releasing code or the constructed benchmarks, though the design relies on multiple specific model checkpoints and fine-tuning procedures described in the appendix.

strengths: The problem of instance-level personalization for frozen VLAs is clearly formulated and well-motivated; the paper convincingly argues that language alone is a fundamental bottleneck for personalized commands like 'bring my cup'.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this line of work: two new simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench) plus a real-robot benchmark on an SO-101 arm, spanning three embodiments (Google Robot, WidowX, Franka, SO-101) and both selection and pick-and-place tasks.

Baselines are constructed carefully and fairly: the Soft Prompt (token-learning) baseline is adapted from Yo'LLaVA with oracle hard negatives from the deployment distribution and >95% recognition accuracy, and the token-embedding transfer assumption is explicitly validated (Appendix B.2, Table 8), which strengthens the credibility of the negative results for token learning.

The main results (e.g., SR 8.5% -> 60.3% on pen holder; 71.3% vs 0-8.3% on WidowX shaver task) show large, consistent gains over generic and prompt-based baselines across all four benchmarks, and the CMR metric usefully separates correct-instance interaction from task completion.

The error analysis (Sec. 5.5, Appendix D) is honest and diagnostic, decomposing failures into single-view grounding errors, multi-view inconsistency, and control failures, with quantitative breakdowns (Table 9); limitations are discussed openly rather than hidden.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: VAP is an assembly of off-the-shelf components (Grounding DINO proposals, DINOv2 embedding voting, SAM2 segmentation/tracking, a semi-transparent tint overlay, and a string-matching instruction rewrite). Each ingredient exists; the paper's claim of 'top-down attention' is largely a framing device, and the core mechanism reduces to standard visual prompting with a detector-verified mask.

The instruction-rewrite template ('my cup' -> 'the red cup') is brittle and under-analyzed: the method implicitly relies on the tint color being a discriminative referring expression, yet there is no ablation of tint color choice, no study of what happens when a distractor shares the tint color, and no comparison against rewriting without the visual overlay (or vice versa) to isolate which component drives the gains.

Grounding accuracy of the perception pipeline itself is never reported in isolation; SR/CMR conflate retrieval errors with manipulation failures, making it hard to attribute the improvements to the matching stage versus the highlight+rewrite alone.

Scale and diversity are modest: only 2 personal categories on Fractal, 4 on Bridge, 5 on VLABench, 8 real-world categories with a single target and two distractors each; real-world results use only 20 trials per task with no variance or significance reporting, so differences like 56.2% vs 45.0% CMR are not clearly separated from noise.

The dominant failure mode in multi-view settings (cross-view mask inconsistency, 50-59% of failures) is identified but not addressed at all; per-view independent grounding is a known-weak design that the authors defer to future work, which limits the method's readiness for the multi-camera setups that motivated the design.

The π0.5 backbone is fine-tuned on task-specific data for VLABench and the real world; while the adaptation data is described as personal-object-free and shared across methods, the interaction between this adaptation and the visual prompting mechanism is not analyzed (e.g., whether VAP gains shrink with a stronger generic backbone).

Several result anomalies go unexplained, e.g., baseline π0 achieving CMR 80.6% but SR 27.8% on Task 6, and Hard Prompts reaching 0.0 CMR/SR on the shaver task while Soft Prompt gets 25.0/8.3, which invites questions about episode construction and metric definitions.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: personalizing frozen VLAs to manipulate user-specific objects among visually similar distractors is a practically important gap that current VLA benchmarks do not test, and the paper articulates the 'control gap' relative to prior personalization work (VLAS, PIN, MEMENTO) convincingly.

The proposed VAP method is simple, training-free, and deployable: reference images form a non-parametric memory, grounding is done with open-vocabulary detection + embedding voting across reference views, and the mask is injected via a semi-transparent highlight plus a template-based instruction rewrite. No VLA parameters change, so new objects are usable immediately after registration.

Comprehensive evaluation across two newly constructed simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench) and a real-world SO-101 setup, spanning two robots (π0) and π0.5, multiple task types, and consistent metrics (SR and the useful CMR). VAP shows large gains on the hardest disambiguation tasks (e.g., CMR 10.5→89.2 on pen holder; SR 0→71.3 on WidowX shaver).

Baselines are treated unusually fairly: the token-learning (Soft Prompt) baseline is built carefully with oracle hard negatives drawn from the deployment distribution and >95% recognition accuracy, and the appendix provides a principled defense of the VLM→VLA token transfer proxy (Table 8 embedding-space analysis) plus attention-heatmap diagnostics explaining why token learning fails at control.

Honest and informative limitations/error analysis: Table 6/9 disentangles grounding failures from manipulation failures, cross-view inconsistency is identified as the dominant multi-view failure mode, and the conclusion and Appendix E scope the contribution to single-object, short-horizon tabletop tasks without overclaiming.
Runtime overhead is measured (0.26s init, ~10% per-step overhead), addressing a practical deployment concern.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: VAP is a pipeline composition of existing off-the-shelf components (Grounding DINO, DINOv2, SAM2) plus visual prompting ideas already explored in robotics (RoboGround, MOKA, PIVOT). The genuinely new element is reference-image-based instance retrieval feeding pixel-space prompts, which is somewhat incremental; the 'top-down attention' cognitive framing is largely rhetorical.

Some results show modest margins where it matters: on Task 2 (bottle) VAP's SR 60.6/58.2 is essentially on par with Hard Prompt (58.8/54.2), and on Personalized-VLABench the cup task gain over Soft Prompt is ~6 points. Real-world absolute success rates (56.2% avg pick-and-place) remain moderate, indicating the pipeline does not fully solve instance-conditioned control.

Evaluation is restricted to a single backbone family (π0/π0.5); it is unclear how VAP transfers to other VLAs with different vision encoders or instruction formats, which weakens the generality claim that this is a generic 'perceptual adapter' for frozen VLAs.

Scenarios are relatively easy for the grounding side: only 2 same-category distractors per episode, single personal object, tabletop, short-horizon tasks. The core claim (instance-level disambiguation) would be more convincing with denser distractor clutter, multiple personal objects, or longer horizons; the authors acknowledge this only partially.

Reproducibility is not fully assured: while experimental details are extensive (Appendix A, prompts in A.3), the paper does not state that code, benchmark assets, or 3D models will be released, which is significant given the contribution's weight on two new benchmarks.

The Soft Prompt baseline is necessarily a proxy (tokens learned in PaliGemma and transferred), and although Appendix B defends it well, a direct comparison against an image-conditioning VLM planner that can see the reference images at inference (e.g., a PIVOT-style loop) is missing; such a baseline would more directly test whether pixel-space prompting is superior to VLM-based disambiguation with references.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: instance-level (personal object) manipulation for VLAs, which existing benchmarks and methods do not address; the framing of personalization as inference-time input optimization rather than model adaptation is sensible.

The proposed VAP is simple, practical, and training-free: reference-image memory (DINOv2 matching), open-vocabulary detection (Grounding DINO), SAM2 tracking, mask-aligned visual highlight, and template-based instruction rewrite, with negligible runtime overhead (0.02s/step).

Comprehensive evaluation across two new simulation benchmarks and a real SO-101 tabletop setup, spanning three robot platforms, single- and multi-view settings, selection and pick-and-place tasks, with appropriate metrics (SR and CMR) that separate correct-object identification from task completion.

Baselines are treated unusually fairly: the Soft Prompt (token-learning) baseline is deliberately strengthened with Yo'LLaVA-style supervision and oracle hard negatives drawn from the test distractors (admitted as leakage favoring the baseline), making VAP's gains conservative; the token embedding transfer analysis in Appendix B is a careful justification of the proxy baseline design.

Extensive ablations (mask+rewrite necessity, voting vs. averaging, number of references K, mask vs. bounding box, opacity sweep) and a candid, well-structured failure taxonomy (single-view grounding errors, multi-view inconsistency, control failures) that honestly attributes a large fraction of failures to cross-view inconsistency and VLA control limits rather than overclaiming.
Careful disclosure of the environment-adaptation fine-tuning of the backbone, with identical frozen policy shared across all baselines, ensuring fair comparison.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: VAP is essentially a system-level combination of off-the-shelf components (Grounding DINO + DINOv2 retrieval + SAM2 tracking + color tint overlay + rule-based instruction rewrite). The core mechanism—'highlight the object in a fixed color and rewrite the instruction to reference that color'—is simple, and the paper does not establish why this specific intervention generalizes beyond the color-attribute bias it exploits.

Strong implicit assumptions narrow the scope: the pipeline presumes the instruction contains a parseable 'my X' span with a known generic category name, that the open-vocabulary detector reliably finds category instances, and that a single fixed tint color is available and not confusable with scene content. These assumptions are only partially discussed, and the deterministic string-matching rewrite is brittle.

Evaluation is restricted to the π-family backbones (π0/π0.5); no evidence that VAP transfers to other VLA architectures (e.g., OpenVLA, RT-2-style models), so the claim of 'personalizing VLAs' may not generalize broadly. The Soft Prompt baseline also uses a proxy transfer from PaliGemma rather than end-to-end token learning in the VLA, which the authors acknowledge but which leaves the strongest competitor slightly untested in its ideal form.

Gains are uneven: on Personalized-VLABench the margins over the strongest baselines are modest (e.g., cup task 60.8 vs. 54.8), and the multi-view inconsistency failure mode accounts for 50–60% of failures in multi-view settings yet is left unimplemented; SR on the Fractal pen-holder task remains only ~60%, indicating substantial headroom.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no explicit statement of code/benchmark release is provided for the two new benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench), which are central to the contribution; reliance on GPT-5.1-generated descriptions and proprietary tools adds reproduction friction.

The dominant failure mode (multi-view inconsistency from independent per-view grounding) is a direct consequence of a core design choice (per-view factorization for real-time inference), and the appendix treatment is largely a future-work sketch (MAP-style association) rather than a mitigation, weakening the robustness of the multi-view results.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: personalized ('my cup') manipulation among same-category distractors is a real gap in current VLA evaluations, and the paper articulates why language-only disambiguation is brittle.

Substantial and multi-faceted evaluation: two newly constructed simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench) plus a real-world SO-101 setup spanning selection and pick-and-place tasks, with consistent gains over generic, hard-prompt, and token-learning baselines (e.g., Table 2: SR 60.3% vs 8.5% baseline).

Unusually rigorous treatment of the strongest baseline: the Soft Prompt (token learning) baseline is strengthened with oracle hard negatives drawn from the actual test-time distractors, achieving >95% recognition accuracy, and the paper openly acknowledges this is a leakage-like setting favorable to the baseline.

Good analysis beyond headline numbers: failure-mode taxonomy (Table 6/9), attention heatmaps explaining why token learning fails in closed loop (Appendix B.3), sensitivity to reference count K, opacity/mask-vs-box ablations, and runtime analysis showing only 0.02 s/step overhead.

Honest limitations discussion: multi-view inconsistency is identified as a dominant failure mode (~50-59% of failures in multi-view settings), and the appendix offers a serious formal treatment of cross-view association even though it is left unimplemented.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: VAP is essentially a pipeline of off-the-shelf components (Grounding DINO for proposals, DINOv2 embeddings for matching, SAM2 for tracking, a fixed-color tint overlay, and a string-match instruction rewrite 'my X' -> 'the red X'). Mark/box-based visual prompting for manipulation and reference-image conditioning already exist (Moka, PIVOT, RoboGround, PIN, MEMENTO); the contribution is a recombination applied to instance disambiguation rather than a new method or insight.

The grounding module arguably does all the intellectual work, making the VLA component nearly vacuous: once only the target is tinted a distinctive color and the instruction rewritten to 'the red cup', the policy faces a trivially disambiguated single-target task. The paper does not clearly separate the contribution of instance matching from the contribution of simply recoloring/highlighting one object; a 'highlight a random same-category object' or 'highlight a non-target object' control would test whether the gains reflect personalization at all.

Benchmarks are small and task diversity is thin: only 2 personal categories on Google Robot, 4 on WidowX, 5 on VLABench, and 8 real categories with just 3 physical instances each (1 target + 2 distractors). Claims of 'instance-level generalization' rest on a small object set, and no statistical significance or variance is reported for the simulation results.

Fixed-color highlighting and rewriting introduce unstated brittleness: conflicts between the tint color and the object's true color, red distractors in the scene, or overlapping highlight and grasp-relevant appearance cues are never analyzed, even though the method's central mechanism is precisely this overlay.

The claimed framing as 'input-side adapter'/'visual attentive prompting' oversells what is a detection-then-recolor cascade; failures dominated by Case 3 (correct prompt but failed manipulation, 78-87% of single-view failures) indicate the approach largely reduces to the VLA's existing competence, and the method contributes little to actual control.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no explicit statement that code or the new benchmarks will be released; evaluation pipelines involve numerous tuned choices (voting rule, opacity, rewrite templates, fallback behaviors) whose implementations would be difficult to reconstruct.

Some writing/claims are inflated relative to evidence, e.g., describing the method as bridging 'semantic understanding and instance-level control' when, per the failure analysis, roughly half or more of VAP's remaining failures are plain manipulation failures, and cross-view consistency-a core requirement for the multi-view benchmarks-is acknowledged to be unsolved.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely practical and underexplored problem: instance-level personalization of frozen VLAs ('my cup' among lookalikes), which existing benchmarks and baselines do not cover. The task formulation is clear and well-motivated.

VAP is simple, training-free, and well-engineered; the language-vision coupling (mask highlight + aligned instruction rewrite) is a sensible design, and the rewrite-only negative control in Appendix E.1 convincingly shows the gains do not come from language cueing alone.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: two adapted simulation benchmarks plus a real SO-101 benchmark across selection and pick-and-place tasks, with a strong baseline suite (generic VLA, LLM-generated hard prompts, and a token-learning baseline deliberately strengthened with oracle hard negatives sampled from test-time distractors — an honest and conservative choice).

Ablations are thorough and cover the design space: rewriting necessity, voting vs. averaging, sensitivity to reference count K (1–7), mask vs. bounding box, and overlay opacity, with a saliency–occlusion trade-off analysis.

Failure analysis is honest and diagnostic: the three-case taxonomy (single-view grounding error, cross-view inconsistency, control failure) with quantitative breakdowns, plus the token-embedding and attention analysis in Appendix B that explains why the token baseline underperforms despite >95% VQA accuracy.

Runtime analysis (0.02s/step tracking overhead) and multi-user sequential execution (Appendix F) demonstrate practical deployability; the limitations discussion is candid (multi-view inconsistency left unaddressed, reliance on off-the-shelf perception).
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the method is a pipeline of off-the-shelf components (Grounding DINO, DINOv2 [CLS] matching, SAM2 tracking, color overlay, template string rewrite). The core insight — that frozen VLAs can exploit a color-highlighted mask plus a rewritten instruction — is empirical rather than a new technique, which may constrain the paper's appeal at a main ML venue.

The method leaves substantial headroom unaddressed: on Google Robot, SR remains 60–62% against ~84–89% CMR, and Case 3 (correct grounding, failed manipulation) dominates failures (86.9%/78.6% in single-view settings). Multi-view inconsistency — the largest failure mode (59.2%/50.9% of failures) — is only sketched as future work (Appendix D.2), so the central limitation is deferred rather than solved.

The grounding step requires parsing the instruction into 'my X', assumes the category name is known and detectable, and depends on the mask tint color being describable and groundable by the VLA. Robustness to free-form personalized language, occlusion of the target, or instances indistinguishable in color space is not evaluated.

Some evaluation caveats: real-world results use 20 trials per task with standard deviations reported only across (not within) tasks; the hard prompt baselines perform surprisingly poorly (often near-generic levels), and while GPT-generated descriptions are provided, it is hard to fully verify the baseline was as strong as the token baseline was made to be.
Several references are anachronistic/dated 2026 (e.g., HuggingFace 2026, Sketchfab 2026, Ren 2026), and the use of 'GPT-5.1' for baseline descriptions is under-specified; these should be cleaned up.

The claim that gains 'persist under variant aggregation' is weaker than in visual matching (SR 58.2% vs. 60.3% with larger CMR-SR gaps), and the Bridge benchmark has only 96 base episodes, limiting statistical strength in some cells.
